abstracts.abstract: The rapid accumulation of multi-omics data has exposed fundamental limitations in existing frameworks for biological network inference, which predominantly rely on pairwise correlation metrics that fail to capture higher-order interactions among biological molecules. We introduce a novel information-theoretic framework termed Higher-Order Interaction Decomposition (HOID) that conceptualizes biological systems as hypergraphs where interactions extend beyond dyadic relationships. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that conventional network representations systematically underestimate the contribution of combinatorial molecular features to phenotypic variation, resulting in prediction errors that propagate through downstream systems biology analyses. The HOID framework introduces a mathematically rigorous decomposition of mutual information into hierarchical interaction components, enabling the identification of statistically significant higher-order effects that remain undetected by existing approaches. Through rigorous analysis of synthetic and real-world transcriptomic datasets, we establish that approximately 35% of functionally relevant gene interactions exhibit non-dyadic characteristics that cannot be adequately characterized by traditional methods. This work fundamentally reframes how we conceptualize molecular interaction networks and provides a theoretical foundation for next-generation computational biology approaches that embrace the inherent complexity of biological systems.

Protein contact prediction has long relied on direct coupling analysis (DCA) methods derived from statistical mechanics principles, yet current implementations exhibit systematic biases when applied to proteins with non-uniform sequence sampling across phylogenetic lineages. We present an Enhanced DCA (EDCA) framework that substantially improves contact prediction accuracy through three theoretical innovations: first, a phylogenetically weighted sequence reweighting scheme that corrects for uneven taxonomic sampling; second, a novel pseudocount estimation approach based on mixture modeling of site-specific evolutionary rates; and third, an adaptive regularization method that accounts for varying sequence coverage across protein families. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that EDCA reduces the effective number of independent sequences required for reliable predictions by approximately 40% compared to standard DCA approaches. Validation on CASP13 and CASP14 targets demonstrates that EDCA achieves a mean precision of 72.3% for top-L/5 predicted contacts, representing a 12.7% improvement over state-of-the-art methods on datasets with uneven phylogenetic representation. This work provides both theoretical insights into the relationship between sequence sampling and evolutionary signal extraction and practical tools that extend the applicability of DCA-based methods to challenging protein families with limited or biased sequence information.

The integration of single-cell transcriptomics with spatial profiling technologies has emerged as a central challenge in computational biology, yet existing computational pipelines lack the ability to perform truly integrated analysis that preserves the unique information content of each modality. We present SpatialTranscriptomeAI (STAI), a comprehensive computational platform that implements a novel multi-modal fusion architecture based on graph neural networks operating on a unified spatial gene expression manifold. Unlike previous approaches that rely on late-stage integration or require explicit correspondence between modalities, STAI employs a contrastive learning framework that discovers intrinsic structural relationships across spatial and single-cell data without requiring paired observations. The platform incorporates novel attention mechanisms that dynamically weight contributions from different modalities based on local data quality, enabling robust integration even when modalities exhibit missing or inconsistent measurements. STAI provides end-to-end functionality including quality control, batch effect correction, cell type deconvolution, spatial domain identification, and interactive visualization. Benchmarking across 15 public spatial transcriptomics datasets demonstrates that STAI consistently outperforms existing integration methods, achieving a 28% improvement in cell type assignment accuracy and enabling the discovery of spatially localized gene programs that remain undetected by single-modality analyses.

Clinical interpretation of genomic variants remains bottlenecked by the lack of scalable systems capable of integrating heterogeneous evidence sources to assess pathogenicity. We present PathoFlow 2.0, a substantially enhanced clinical variant interpretation system that addresses critical limitations of its predecessor through four major architectural improvements: first, a transformer-based variant representation learning module that captures contextual sequence information with unprecedented fidelity; second, a novel evidence retrieval system that dynamically queries 23 clinical and functional databases with adaptive relevance ranking; third, an uncertainty-aware pathogenicity scoring framework that provides calibrated confidence estimates alongside predictions; and fourth, a federated learning architecture enabling collaborative model improvement across institutions without sharing sensitive patient data. PathoFlow 2.0 introduces standardized APIs for seamless integration with laboratory information systems and electronic health records, facilitating deployment in clinical genomics workflows. Retrospective validation on 45,000 variants from multiple clinical cohorts demonstrates that PathoFlow 2.0 achieves an AUC of 0.94 for pathogenicity classification, representing a 15% improvement over existing clinical tools, while substantially reducing inter-annotator variability through more consistent evidence synthesis. The system has been deployed at 12 clinical sites, processing over 8,000 variants monthly with validated improvement in diagnostic yield for rare disease patients.
